brief.studentFacingIntro:
In this assignment you will build and audit a small workplace-style Excel model used for pricing and planning. You will demonstrate correct use of units, rounding and significant figures; rearrange formulae to isolate key variables; design an auditable spreadsheet using robust referencing and naming; and test whether production targets are feasible under stated constraints. Your submission must be understandable to a colleague who did not build the model, and must include clear assumptions and a traceable change record.

Hybrid delivery: you may attend live sessions in person or online. You may present your walkthrough live or submit a recording. Where collaboration is used (peer review), an asynchronous alternative is provided.
brief.workplaceContext:
You work in operations support for a small manufacturer producing two products (Product A and Product B). Your manager needs an auditable Excel workbook that (1) calculates unit cost and price, (2) allows quick “what-if” changes (e.g., wage rate, material usage, scrap), (3) shows the effect of rounding choices and tolerances on final price, and (4) checks whether a proposed weekly production plan is feasible given labour and material limits.

The workbook will be shared internally and may be checked during an audit, so the layout, documentation, and change notes must be clear.
stepByStepInstructions: Step 1 — Download and read the assignment template pack from the LMS (or collect a printed copy in class). The pack contains: (a) scenario data tables, (b) required sheet structure, (c) a change log table format, and (d) a self-audit checklist.

Step 2 — Set up your Excel workbook structure with separate tabs (minimum): Inputs, Calculations, Outputs, Audit_Log, and Feasibility. Use a consistent layout, clear headings, and cell styling that distinguishes inputs from calculated cells.

Step 3 — Define units for every input and key output (e.g., £/hr, kg/unit, units/week). Record units next to inputs and in output tables. Where you convert units (e.g., minutes to hours; grams to kg), show the conversion clearly in the calculations.

Step 4 — Implement significant figures and rounding rules appropriate to a workplace context (e.g., money to 2 d.p.; measured quantities to a stated precision). Create a short “Rounding & Precision Policy” section in your workbook (either on Outputs or Audit_Log) explaining your choices.

Step 5 — Demonstrate error propagation through a multi-step spreadsheet: choose at least two measured inputs with tolerances/uncertainty (provided in the scenario pack), and show how these tolerances affect a final output (e.g., unit cost or contribution margin). Use clear formulas and show intermediate steps so the propagation is traceable.

Step 6 — Apply algebraic rearrangement to isolate variables in pricing/production formulae. You must include at least two rearrangements (e.g., solve for required selling price given target margin; solve for required output quantity given fixed costs and desired profit). Implement each rearranged formula in Excel and label it clearly. Record units, rounding choices and assumptions alongside each.

Step 7 — Build the model using robust Excel practices: (a) use correct relative/absolute referencing, (b) create named ranges for key inputs, and (c) use structured layout so the calculation logic can be followed. Avoid hard-coded numbers inside formulas (except 0/1 flags where justified).

Step 8 — Create an audit trail: complete the Audit_Log tab with traceable change notes. Include at least five change entries (e.g., correction of a unit, update to a rounding rule, renamed range, fixed reference, revised assumption). Each entry must include date/time (or version), what changed, why, and impact.

Step 9 — Feasibility check: using linear equations and inequalities, test whether a proposed production target is feasible under constraints provided (e.g., labour hours, material availability, machine time). Show the inequalities and the logic used to determine feasibility. If infeasible, show at least one feasible alternative plan (e.g., revised mix or reduced total) and explain it.

Step 10 — Prepare your written audit note and walkthrough. Your audit note should explain how your workbook works, highlight units/rounding decisions, summarise the error propagation demonstration, and present the feasibility conclusion with assumptions.

Step 11 — Peer review (collaborative element) OR asynchronous alternative: Option A (collaborative): exchange your workbook (or PDF printout) with one peer in your seminar group and provide structured feedback using the checklist (upload your feedback as evidence). Option B (asynchronous): complete the self-audit checklist yourself and write a brief note identifying at least three risks or improvements you would make if this were a live business tool.

Step 12 — Submit all required deliverables by the deadline using digital submission (LMS upload) or physical submission (printed report and spreadsheet printouts) as agreed with the tutor. If submitting physically, you must also provide the Excel file on a USB drive or via LMS upload unless a reasonable adjustment is in place.

rubric.criterionName: Units, significant figures, rounding rules and error propagation
rubric.fail: Units are missing or inconsistent for multiple inputs/outputs; rounding is applied inconsistently or not justified; explanations are absent or incorrect; error propagation is not demonstrated, is conceptually incorrect, or cannot be traced through the spreadsheet steps.
rubric.pass: Units are stated for key inputs and outputs with only minor omissions; rounding and significant figures are generally appropriate for money and measured quantities and are stated in a brief policy; an error propagation example is included and mostly traceable, showing how input tolerance affects at least one final output.
rubric.merit: Units are consistently recorded for all relevant inputs and outputs; rounding/significant figures choices are clearly justified with workplace rationale; error propagation is clearly set out with traceable intermediate steps and a correct explanation of how rounding/precision affects final figures.
rubric.distinction: Units are comprehensive and include clear conversions where needed; rounding/significant figures policy is precise, consistently implemented, and explicitly linked to decision-making (e.g., pricing impact); error propagation is demonstrated clearly across multiple steps with a well-explained sensitivity/tolerance impact and transparent auditability.

rubric.criterionName: Algebraic rearrangement and implementation in Excel with documentation
rubric.fail: Rearrangements are missing or incorrect; Excel formulas do not reflect correct rearranged relationships; units, rounding choices, and assumptions are not recorded or are contradictory; the model cannot be used to isolate variables reliably.
rubric.pass: At least two correct algebraic rearrangements are included and implemented in Excel; variables are isolated to support pricing/production questions; units and key assumptions are recorded, with rounding choices stated but not always fully justified.
rubric.merit: Rearrangements are correct, clearly labelled, and implemented using good Excel practice (e.g., named ranges, no hard-coded constants unless justified); units, rounding choices, and assumptions are clearly documented next to the relevant calculations.
rubric.distinction: Rearrangements are correct and used effectively for realistic scenarios (e.g., target margin/profit, break-even-style reasoning); documentation is thorough and audit-ready (units, rounding, assumptions, and limits of validity are explicit); Excel implementation supports easy what-if changes without breaking logic.

rubric.criterionName: Spreadsheet transparency, referencing, named ranges, structured layout and audit change notes
rubric.fail: Workbook layout is confusing; formulas contain hard-coded values without explanation; referencing is incorrect or fragile (e.g., broken relative/absolute references); named ranges are absent or misused; change notes are missing or not traceable.
rubric.pass: Workbook follows a mostly clear structure with separate inputs/calculations/outputs; referencing is mostly correct; some named ranges are used; an Audit_Log is included with at least five entries that broadly describe changes.
rubric.merit: Workbook is clearly structured and readable; inputs are clearly separated and protected/marked; referencing is robust (appropriate absolute/relative use); named ranges are used for key inputs; Audit_Log entries are specific (what/why/impact) and enable traceability for review.
rubric.distinction: Workbook demonstrates strong spreadsheet engineering: consistent layout conventions, transparent calculation flow, reliable referencing throughout, well-chosen named ranges, and outputs designed for quick checking; Audit_Log is detailed and supports an audit narrative (including versioning and clear impact statements).

rubric.criterionName: Linear equations/inequalities feasibility testing and clear assumptions
rubric.fail: Feasibility test is missing or incorrect; constraints are not expressed as linear equations/inequalities or are misapplied; assumptions are absent; feasibility conclusion is unsupported or contradictory to the model’s numbers.
rubric.pass: Constraints are expressed as linear equations/inequalities and used to test feasibility of the target plan; conclusion (feasible/infeasible) is mostly correct; assumptions are stated but may be brief or incomplete; at least one feasible adjustment is suggested if infeasible.
rubric.merit: Feasibility test correctly applies linear equations/inequalities with clear working; assumptions are clearly documented and consistent with the spreadsheet; conclusion is well supported; where infeasible, an alternative feasible plan is shown with clear reasoning.
rubric.distinction: Feasibility analysis is rigorous and clearly communicated: constraints are correctly defined and checked, assumptions are explicit and well-justified, and the feasibility conclusion is presented in a way suitable for team review (including a clear alternative plan and explanation of trade-offs).

sectionA.questionText: A production team uses the profit model Profit = (P − v)Q − F, where P is selling price (£/unit), v is variable cost (£/unit), Q is units sold (units), and F is fixed cost (£). For the next batch: v = £12/unit, F = £18,000, Q = 2,500 units. What selling price P is required to achieve a target Profit of £7,500? Round to the nearest penny and state the unit in your answer choice.

A site produces two products, X and Y. Each unit of X uses 2 machine-hours and 1 assembly-hour. Each unit of Y uses 1 machine-hour and 3 assembly-hours. Weekly available capacity is 100 machine-hours and 120 assembly-hours. Assuming both constraints bind, how many units of (X, Y) satisfy the system exactly?

2X + 1Y = 100
1X + 3Y = 120

In a costing spreadsheet, variable cost is £0.08 per gram. Quantity is entered in kilograms in cell B5. Which Excel-style formula correctly calculates variable cost in £ (with correct unit conversion)?
sectionA.rationale: £0.08 per gram must multiply grams. If B5 is kg, grams = B5×1000, so cost = 0.08×(B5×1000). The other options incorrectly scale by 1/1000 or omit conversion.

sectionA.questionText: Throughput after maintenance is modelled (from operational data) by T(d) = −0.5d^2 + 8d + 60, where d is days after maintenance and T is units/hour. On which day does the model predict maximum throughput?
options: D) The model has no maximum
sectionA.rationale: For a quadratic ax^2+bx+c with a<0, the maximum occurs at d = −b/(2a) = −8/(2×−0.5) = 8.

sectionA.questionText:
Revenue and cost for a service are modelled as:
R(q) = 40q − 0.02q^2 (in £ per period)
C(q) = 5,000 + 18q (in £ per period)
where q is the number of jobs completed per period. Based on these functions, for which range of q is profit positive (i.e., R(q) − C(q) > 0)?
options: A) Profit is positive for all q > 0
B) Profit is positive for no q (never breaks even)
C) Profit is positive approximately for 321 ≤ q ≤ 779
D) Profit is positive approximately for q ≥ 779 only
sectionA.rationale: Profit π(q)=R−C= (40q−0.02q^2)−(5000+18q)=22q−0.02q^2−5000. Solve −0.02q^2+22q−5000>0. Roots of 0.02q^2−22q+5000=0 are q≈320.87 and q≈779.13, so profit is positive between the roots.

sectionA.questionText: A process cost is modelled as C(q) = 1,200 + 5q + 0.04q^2 (C in £/day, q in units/day). What is the marginal cost at q = 100 units/day? Give the answer in £ per additional unit (i.e., £/unit).
sectionA.rationale: Marginal cost is derivative: C'(q)=5+0.08q. At q=100: 5+8=13 (£/unit).

sectionA.questionText:
Demand is modelled by price p(q) = 50 − 0.05q (£/unit). Daily cost is C(q) = 1,000 + 20q (£/day), where q is units/day. Profit is π(q) = p(q)·q − C(q).

(a) Find the production level q that maximises profit.
(b) Compute the maximum profit at this q.

Give q in units/day (whole number) and profit in £/day (nearest £).
A tank is filled with a flow rate r(t) = 2 + 0.5t litres/minute, where t is minutes from the start. How much volume is added over the first 10 minutes?
A manager asks what “marginal cost at q = 500” means for the cost function C(q). Which explanation is correct for audit-friendly reporting?
options: A) The average cost per unit when producing 500 units
B) The total cost when producing 500 units
C) The approximate change in total cost for producing one additional unit when output is around 500 units
D) The maximum possible cost at 500 units
sectionA.rationale: Marginal cost is dC/dq, interpreted locally as the rate of change of total cost with respect to output; it approximates the cost of producing one more unit near that output level.

sectionA.questionText: You are using Excel Solver to minimise total weekly labour cost. Decision variables are the number of hours assigned to Team A and Team B. The model has a required total of at least 400 hours and each team has a maximum availability (A ≤ 260, B ≤ 220). Which Solver setup is correct?
options: A) Set Objective: total hours; To: Min; By Changing: hourly rates; Subject to: costs ≥ 400
B) Set Objective: total cost; To: Min; By Changing: Team A hours and Team B hours; Subject to: A + B ≥ 400, A ≤ 260, B ≤ 220
C) Set Objective: total cost; To: Max; By Changing: Team A hours and Team B hours; Subject to: A + B ≤ 400
D) Set Objective: total cost; To: Min; By Changing: A + B; Subject to: A ≤ 260, B ≤ 220
sectionA.rationale: Objective should be the cost cell, minimised. Changing cells must be the decision variables (A and B hours). Constraints reflect the requirement and capacity limits.

sectionA.questionText:
A quality engineer samples n = 16 parts and measures a critical dimension. The sample mean is x̄ = 12.4 mm and sample standard deviation is s = 0.8 mm. Assuming approximate normality, compute a 95% confidence interval for the true mean dimension (use a t critical value t0.975,15 = 2.131).

Give your interval to 2 d.p. in mm.
You report a 95% confidence interval for the mean fill volume as [498 ml, 502 ml]. Which statement is the most accurate for non-specialist stakeholders?
options: A) There is a 95% probability that the true mean is between 498 ml and 502 ml
B) If we repeated the same sampling method many times, about 95% of the intervals we compute would contain the true mean
C) 95% of individual units have fill volume between 498 ml and 502 ml
D) The mean fill volume is exactly 500 ml
sectionA.rationale: A confidence interval is a procedure with long-run coverage properties; it does not assign a probability to a fixed parameter after observing the data.

sectionA.questionText: A process lead wants to understand whether increasing oven temperature is associated with higher defect rate. You have paired data (temperature setting, defect %). Which visual is most appropriate for an evidence-based explanation in a quality report?
options: A) Pie chart of defect categories
B) Scatter plot of defect % against temperature, with a fitted trendline
D) Stacked bar chart of weekly totals
sectionA.rationale: A scatter plot directly shows the relationship between two quantitative variables and supports interpretation of trend and strength (optionally with a trendline).

sectionA.questionText: A maintenance analyst models “time between failures” for a component. Times are non-negative and the team assumes failures occur randomly at a roughly constant average rate. Which distribution is the most appropriate starting point for time between events?
sectionA.rationale: Under a constant hazard (Poisson process assumption), inter-arrival times are modelled with an exponential distribution; it is non-negative and right-skewed.

sectionA.questionText:
A delivery task duration is modelled as Normally distributed with mean 10.0 days and standard deviation 1.5 days. What is the probability the task takes longer than 12.0 days? Use the standard normal CDF value Φ(1.33) ≈ 0.9082.

Give your final probability to 3 decimal places.

A Monte Carlo cost simulation (10,000 runs) reports: mean cost = £1.10m, P90 cost = £1.25m. A finance manager asks for a budget that has approximately a 90% chance of not being exceeded (based on this model). What budget recommendation best matches the request?
options: A) Budget £1.10m because it is the expected cost
B) Budget £1.25m because it is the 90th percentile (P90)
C) Budget £1.35m because it is higher than P90
D) Budget £0.15m because it is the contingency amount only
sectionA.rationale: A 90% non-exceedance budget corresponds to the 90th percentile of simulated outcomes; therefore use the P90 value (£1.25m).

sectionA.questionText: You are updating a workplace risk register entry for a schedule-risk simulation. Which set of items is MOST appropriate to record to meet good practice on assumptions, uncertainty and limitations?
options: A) Only the final P90 date, with no other notes
B) The software version only, because results are reproducible
C) Input distributions and parameter sources, key assumptions (e.g., independence/correlation), number of simulation runs, and main limitations (e.g., data quality, model scope)
D) A screenshot of the output chart only
sectionA.rationale: Audit-friendly risk reporting requires documenting assumptions, uncertainty sources and limitations, plus enough detail to understand and reproduce the simulation (inputs, run settings, and scope constraints).

sectionA.questionText: A technician uses the relation Energy = Power × Time. Power is recorded in kW and time is recorded in hours. What are the correct units for the computed energy, and why is this a dimensional check?
options: A) kWh; because kW×h is consistent with energy units and flags unit-mismatch errors (e.g., seconds vs hours)
B) kW/h; because dividing by time gives energy
C) kW; because energy and power have the same units
D) hours; because time dominates the calculation
sectionA.rationale: Dimensional analysis checks unit consistency. kW×h gives kWh, a standard energy unit. Unit mismatches (e.g., using minutes without conversion) would make reported energy incorrect.

sectionA.questionText:
A calibrated model uses the volume of a cylinder V = πr^2h. Measurements are r = 50.0 ± 0.2 mm and h = 120.0 ± 0.5 mm.

Using a first-order tolerance (sensitivity) approximation, estimate:
(a) the nominal volume in cm^3, and
(b) the approximate percentage tolerance on V.

Give V to 2 d.p. (cm^3) and tolerance to 2 d.p. (%).

A one-way sensitivity check varies each input by +10% (one at a time) and records the % change in model output (a cost estimate). Results are:
- Labour rate +10% ⇒ output +6%
- Material price +10% ⇒ output +2%
- Cycle time +10% ⇒ output +9%
- Scrap rate +10% ⇒ output +4%

Which input is MOST influential under this sensitivity check, and what is the best next action for validation documentation?
options: A) Material price; stop analysis because +2% is small
B) Cycle time; document this as a key driver and prioritise validating cycle-time measurement and assumptions
C) Labour rate; remove labour from the model to simplify it
D) Scrap rate; round all results to whole numbers to reduce noise
sectionA.rationale: The largest output response is from cycle time (+9%), indicating highest sensitivity in this check. Good validation practice is to document sensitivity results and prioritise verifying the most influential inputs (data source, measurement method, and assumptions).

sectionC.taskDescription: Model validation and sensitivity audit for a production cost model. You have been asked to evaluate whether the current energy–throughput model is suitable for audit use and to create an improved, reproducible calculation log. The process produces good units Q per week by running a machine at speed v (units/hour) for H hours with scrap rate r. Good output is modelled by Q = vH(1 − r). Energy consumption is modelled by E = k v^2 H (kWh), where k is an unknown calibration constant. Energy cost is Ce = Pe · E, where Pe is the electricity price (£/kWh). Two weeks of operational data are provided: Week A: v = 80, H = 35, r = 0.06, energy bill = £1,960. Week B: v = 90, H = 35, r = 0.08, energy bill = £2,550. Assume Pe = £0.25/kWh and that the energy bill corresponds to Ce only (ignore standing charges).
instructions: Create a spreadsheet (or Python notebook) that calculates Q, E and Ce for each week and back-solves k from Week A and Week B. Show each step clearly and label units in cells/columns.

Evaluate the consistency of k across the two weeks. Decide whether a single calibrated k is acceptable for audit use. Justify your decision quantitatively (e.g., percentage difference) and qualitatively (assumptions, likely causes of variation).
Perform dimensional/units checks on Q and E. Identify any implicit unit requirements for k and state them explicitly.

Create a sensitivity table for the calibrated model showing the impact on Ce and Q of the following uncertainties (one at a time, holding other inputs constant): v ± 2 units/hour, r ± 0.5 percentage points, Pe ± 10%. Present results with appropriate rounding and clearly stated assumptions.

Propose and document at least two improvements to make the model more robust and reproducible for technical documentation (e.g., tolerance handling, structured calculation log, input validation, version control notes).
sectionC.modelAnswer: A complete response (i) computes Q and solves k using k = (Ce/Pe)/(v^2 H) for each week, (ii) compares k_A and k_B and evaluates whether the discrepancy is acceptable (e.g., reporting percentage difference and discussing sources such as non-energy charges, non-quadratic dependence, changing load, measurement error), (iii) states unit consistency: Q in units/week (or units, given H in hours) and E in kWh, requiring k to carry units of kWh/(units^2·hour), (iv) provides a clear sensitivity table with recalculated Ce and Q under each perturbation, with rounding justified and units shown, and (v) proposes improvements such as separating inputs/outputs, using named ranges, adding data validation for r ∈ [0,1], logging assumptions, and documenting rounding rules and calibration date; optional improvement includes calibrating k via least squares if more weeks are available and recording uncertainty bands for k.
assessmentCriteria: Correct calibration of k from both weeks with clear workings and correct units.
Sound evaluation of calibration consistency and audit suitability, with justified assumptions and limitations.
Dimensional/units checks correctly identified and explicitly documented.
Sensitivity analysis correctly executed, clearly presented, and interpreted (direction and relative impact).
Quality of reproducible documentation: structured log, transparent rounding, and practical improvements proposed.

sectionC.taskDescription: Monte Carlo risk simulation and risk register entry. A small project has three sequential activities with uncertain durations (days): Design ~ Triangular(min 8, mode 10, max 14), Build ~ Normal(mean 20, sd 4) truncated at > 0, Test ~ Triangular(min 6, mode 8, max 12). One team works on one activity at a time. Daily labour cost is £1,200. A contractual penalty of £10,000 is incurred if total duration exceeds 45 days. You must create and evaluate a simulation to quantify schedule and cost risk for a non-specialist project board.
instructions: Using Excel or Python, build a Monte Carlo simulation with at least 5,000 iterations. For each iteration, sample the three activity durations, compute total duration, compute labour cost, and add the penalty if total duration > 45.

Produce and label: (a) a histogram (or density plot) of total duration, (b) a histogram (or density plot) of total cost, and (c) a summary table including mean, standard deviation, P50 and P80 for duration, and expected total cost.
Estimate: (i) P(total duration > 45), (ii) expected penalty cost, and (iii) the P80 schedule (duration) and interpret what P80 means for decision-making.
Construct a 95% confidence interval for expected total cost using an appropriate method (e.g., normal approximation via standard error from simulation, or bootstrap). State and justify the method.
Create a concise risk register entry (4–8 lines) stating key assumptions, the quantified risk, recommended mitigation actions, and limitations/uncertainty in the model.
sectionC.modelAnswer: A complete response (i) implements correct sampling for triangular and truncated normal distributions, runs ≥5,000 iterations, and computes total duration and cost including the conditional penalty, (ii) provides correctly labelled plots and a summary table with appropriate rounding and units, (iii) reports P(duration>45), expected penalty and interprets P80 as a duration with 80% chance of completion by that time under the model, (iv) constructs a justified 95% CI for expected total cost (e.g., mean ± 1.96·SE where SE = s/√n, with a note on Monte Carlo error and distributional assumptions; or bootstrap percentiles), and (v) produces a risk register entry that records assumptions (independence, distribution choice, truncation, sequential working), recommended mitigations (buffer, scope change, parallel resource, supplier escalation), and limitations (distribution fit, lack of correlation, not modelling rework).
assessmentCriteria: Technically correct simulation set-up (distributions, truncation, iteration count) and accurate calculations for duration and cost.
Appropriate and clear visual communication for non-specialist stakeholders (labels, units, interpretation).
Correct risk quantification (probability, expected penalty, P80) and appropriate interpretation for decisions.
Valid confidence interval method with correct computation and clear justification.
Quality of risk register entry: assumptions, mitigations, and limitations recorded clearly and professionally.

sectionC.taskDescription: Pricing and capacity decision: create an evidence-based recommendation using regression, calculus, optimisation and clear communication. Weekly demand data for a product are: price p (£): [12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24]; demand q (units): [5200, 4800, 4400, 3950, 3500, 3000, 2550]. Assume a linear demand model q = a − bp. Variable cost is £7.50 per unit and fixed cost is £12,000 per week. Operational constraints: price must be between £13 and £23 inclusive; weekly capacity is at most 4,300 units. Your task is to create a recommended price and production target with an auditable calculation trail.
instructions: Fit the linear demand model q = a − bp using Excel or Python regression. Report estimated a and b, and include a scatter plot with the fitted line.
Create profit as a function of price: π(p) = p·q(p) − 7.50·q(p) − 12,000, then differentiate to find the unconstrained profit-maximising price. Show algebra and units clearly.

Apply the operational constraints (price bounds and capacity). Determine the feasible recommended price and production target. If the unconstrained optimum violates constraints, justify the constrained optimum selection.

Use Excel Solver (or equivalent) to verify your recommendation by maximising profit subject to the constraints. Include Solver settings (objective, decision variable, constraints) in a calculation log for audit.

Quantify and communicate uncertainty: provide a 95% confidence interval for predicted demand at the recommended price (state method). Provide a one-page management summary (bullet points acceptable) including recommended price, predicted demand, planned production, expected profit, key risks/assumptions, and a clear graph indicating the turning point and constraint region.
sectionC.modelAnswer: A complete response (i) performs linear regression to estimate a and b and presents an appropriate plot, (ii) builds π(p) using q(p) and differentiates to obtain the stationary point p* (typically via setting dπ/dp = 0), (iii) evaluates constraints: checks p* within [13,23] and applies capacity by setting planned production to min(predicted demand, 4,300), selecting the constrained best feasible price by comparing profit at candidates (e.g., p*, boundary values, and any capacity-binding point), (iv) corroborates using Solver with correctly stated objective and constraints and retains an auditable log of settings and outputs, and (v) produces an uncertainty statement with a justified 95% CI for predicted demand (e.g., regression prediction interval/CI using standard error, or an approximate CI with assumptions stated), plus a concise, non-technical management summary and a graph showing the profit curve/turning point and where constraints bind.
assessmentCriteria: Correct regression modelling and interpretation, with appropriate visualisation and parameter reporting.
Correct creation of profit function and differentiation, with a valid unconstrained optimum identified.
Sound constrained decision-making with explicit comparison/justification and correct handling of capacity and price bounds.
Solver verification is correctly configured, reproducible, and logged for audit.
Clear stakeholder communication: uncertainty quantified, assumptions and limitations stated, and visuals/summary suitable for a team review meeting.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
Using Profit = (P − v)Q − F:
• Contribution per unit = (P − v).
• Break-even occurs when Profit = 0, so Q_BE = F/(P − v) (provided P > v).
• Profit increases with Q if P > v; otherwise each additional unit reduces profit.
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying/using the contribution term (P − v) and/or setting Profit = 0; 1 mark for the correct break-even expression Q = F/(P − v) and/or correct interpretation of fixed cost F and variable cost v.

performanceThresholds.fail: Does not correctly identify the meaning of terms in the profit model and cannot form a correct break-even or interpretation statement.
performanceThresholds.pass: Identifies contribution (P − v) or fixed cost F correctly, but break-even expression/interpretation is incomplete or contains a minor error.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correct break-even relationship and correct interpretation of the key parameters (P, v, Q, F) with only minor omission.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Fully correct break-even expression and clear, precise interpretation (including the condition P > v and the managerial meaning of contribution and fixed cost).

sectionA.modelAnswer:
Let x and y be the number of units of products X and Y. If each unit of X uses 2 machine-hours and each unit of Y uses 1 machine-hour, and M machine-hours are available, the machine-hour capacity constraint is:
2x + 1y ≤ M, with x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
(If the question also specifies a second resource, the corresponding linear constraint should be written analogously.)
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for defining decision variables (x, y) appropriately; 1 mark for forming the correct linear capacity constraint in the required resource (e.g., 2x + y ≤ M) including inequality direction and non-negativity.

performanceThresholds.fail: No meaningful constraint or incorrect structure (e.g., wrong coefficients, wrong inequality direction) with no correct variable definition.
performanceThresholds.pass: Correct intent (capacity constraint) but with a minor structural error (e.g., missing non-negativity or minor notation issue).
performanceThresholds.merit: Correct constraint with correct coefficients and inequality direction; variables clearly defined.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Correct constraint(s) with clear variable definitions, correct units, and explicit non-negativity; any additional resource constraint(s) also correctly stated where applicable.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
Total variable cost (£) = 0.08 × (quantity in grams). In Excel, if quantity (grams) is in cell B2, the variable cost formula is:
=0.08*B2
(If quantity is entered in kilograms, it must first be converted to grams: =0.08*(B2*1000).)
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for correct multiplication structure (rate × quantity); 1 mark for correct unit handling (grams vs kg) and/or correct Excel syntax.

performanceThresholds.fail: Formula does not represent variable cost as rate × quantity and/or contains major unit misuse.
performanceThresholds.pass: Correct general structure but with a minor Excel syntax error or unclear unit conversion.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correct Excel formula with correct unit basis as stated in the question.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Correct formula plus explicit recognition/handling of unit conversion where relevant and clear labelling of £ output.

sectionA.modelAnswer: For a linear model T(d) = −0.5d (+ constant if specified), the coefficient −0.5 is the marginal change in throughput per unit increase in d. That is, throughput decreases by 0.5 throughput-units for each 1-unit increase in d (holding other factors constant).
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for identifying −0.5 as the slope/marginal effect; 1 mark for stating the correct direction (decrease) and interpreting in context (per unit of d).

performanceThresholds.fail: Does not recognise the slope/marginal effect or gives the wrong direction of effect.
performanceThresholds.pass: Recognises the slope but provides an incomplete or weak contextual interpretation.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correctly interprets the coefficient as a decrease of 0.5 per unit increase in d, in context.
performanceThresholds.distinction: As merit, plus clearly states the ‘ceteris paribus’ meaning and uses correct units/wording aligned to throughput and d.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
Given R(q) = 40q − 0.02q²:
• Marginal revenue: R′(q) = 40 − 0.04q.
• Revenue is maximised where R′(q)=0 ⇒ 40 − 0.04q = 0 ⇒ q* = 1000.
• Maximum revenue: R(1000) = 40(1000) − 0.02(1000)² = 40,000 − 20,000 = £20,000.
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for correct differentiation (R′(q) = 40 − 0.04q) or correct first-order condition; 1 mark for correct optimal quantity q* = 1000 and/or correct maximum revenue value.

performanceThresholds.fail: Cannot differentiate correctly and does not identify the maximising quantity.
performanceThresholds.pass: Partially correct (e.g., correct derivative but incorrect algebra to solve for q, or correct q but no supporting working).
performanceThresholds.merit: Correct derivative and correct maximising quantity; revenue value may be missing or contain only an arithmetic slip.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Fully correct derivative, maximising quantity, and maximum revenue with clear reasoning (including noting concavity due to negative q² coefficient).

sectionA.modelAnswer:
Given C(q) = 1,200 + 5q + 0.04q²:
• Fixed cost = 1,200.
• Variable cost component = 5q + 0.04q².
• Marginal cost: C′(q) = 5 + 0.08q.
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for identifying fixed and variable components correctly; 1 mark for correct marginal cost via differentiation (C′(q) = 5 + 0.08q) where required by the question.

performanceThresholds.fail: Does not correctly identify fixed/variable parts and cannot produce a correct marginal cost expression.
performanceThresholds.pass: Correctly identifies either fixed cost or marginal cost, but not both (or includes a minor differentiation slip).
performanceThresholds.merit: Correctly identifies fixed cost and provides correct marginal cost expression.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Fully correct with clear economic interpretation (fixed cost, increasing marginal cost due to the quadratic term) and correct units.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
With demand p(q) = 50 − 0.05q, revenue is R(q)=p(q)q=50q−0.05q². Profit is π(q)=R(q)−C(q).
First-order condition for profit maximisation: π′(q)=R′(q)−C′(q)=0.
Here R′(q)=50−0.1q, so the optimal q* solves:
50 − 0.1q* = C′(q*).
Then compute p* = 50 − 0.05q* and profit π(q*) = p*q* − C(q*). (Second-order check: π′′(q)=−0.1−C′′(q)<0 for typical non-decreasing marginal cost.)
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for forming R(q) correctly from p(q) and setting up π(q); 1 mark for stating/using the correct optimality condition MR = MC (i.e., 50 − 0.1q = C′(q)) and indicating how to obtain q* and p* using the given C(q).

performanceThresholds.fail: Does not form revenue/profit correctly and does not state a correct optimisation condition.
performanceThresholds.pass: Correctly forms revenue or states MR=MC, but the setup is incomplete (e.g., missing derivative) or contains a minor algebraic error.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correct setup of profit, correct MR expression, and correct condition to solve for q* using C′(q).
performanceThresholds.distinction: As merit, plus clear completion steps (including second-order condition/concavity reasoning) and correct managerial interpretation of q* and p*.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
Volume added over 0 to t minutes is the integral of the flow rate:
V(t)=∫(2+0.5t)dt = 2t + 0.25t² (litres), assuming V(0)=0.
If asked for the volume in the first 10 minutes: V(10)=2(10)+0.25(10²)=20+25=45 litres.
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for correct integration (antiderivative 2t + 0.25t²); 1 mark for correct evaluation over the stated time interval (e.g., t=10 gives 45 litres).

performanceThresholds.fail: Does not integrate correctly and/or confuses rate with volume.
performanceThresholds.pass: Correct approach (integration) but with a minor arithmetic slip or omission of limits/initial condition.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correct integral and correct numerical evaluation for the stated time period.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Fully correct with clear statement of limits, initial condition, and units (litres).

sectionA.modelAnswer:
‘Marginal cost at q = 500’ means C′(500): the instantaneous rate of change of total cost with respect to output at q=500. Practically, it approximates the additional cost of producing one more unit when current production is about 500 units, i.e.
C(501) − C(500) ≈ C′(500).
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for identifying marginal cost as the derivative C′(q) evaluated at q=500; 1 mark for correct practical interpretation as ‘cost of one additional unit near 500’ (local approximation).

performanceThresholds.fail: Incorrect definition (e.g., average cost) and no valid interpretation.
performanceThresholds.pass: States it is ‘extra cost’ but does not link to derivative/evaluation at 500, or gives a vague interpretation.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correct derivative-based definition and a reasonable practical interpretation.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Precise derivative definition plus correct incremental approximation statement (C(501) − C(500) ≈ C′(500)) and clear context.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
In Excel Solver for minimising total weekly labour cost:
• Objective (Set Objective): the total labour cost cell (to be minimised).
• Decision variables (By Changing Variable Cells): the staffing/labour allocation quantities (e.g., hours per role/shift, number of staff assigned).
• Constraints: required demand/coverage constraints, maximum hours, contractual limits, non-negativity/integrality (if needed).
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the decision variables as the allocation/quantity cells Solver changes; 1 mark for correctly identifying objective and/or typical constraints for a labour-cost minimisation model.

performanceThresholds.fail: Misidentifies decision variables and cannot describe objective/constraints appropriately.
performanceThresholds.pass: Identifies either the objective or decision variables correctly, but not both (or provides only generic statements).
performanceThresholds.merit: Correctly identifies decision variables and objective; mentions at least one appropriate constraint type.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Fully correct identification of objective, decision variables, and a coherent set of relevant constraints (including integrality where appropriate).

sectionA.modelAnswer:
For n = 16 with unknown population standard deviation, a confidence interval for the mean uses the t-distribution with df = 15:
CI: x̄ ± t_{α/2,15} × (s/√16) = x̄ ± t_{α/2,15} × (s/4).
For a 95% CI, use t_{0.975,15}.
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for selecting the correct distribution/df (t with 15 degrees of freedom); 1 mark for the correct CI form x̄ ± t × s/√n (or equivalent).

performanceThresholds.fail: Uses an inappropriate method (e.g., z with unknown σ without justification) and/or incorrect CI structure.
performanceThresholds.pass: Correct general CI idea but missing df or uses an incorrect critical value notation; formula mostly correct.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correct t-based CI with correct df and correct standard error term.
performanceThresholds.distinction: As merit, with clear notation (t_{0.975,15}) and explicit simplification to s/4.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
A 95% confidence interval of [498 ml, 502 ml] means: based on the sample and method used, we are 95% confident that the true population mean fill volume lies between 498 ml and 502 ml.
It does not mean there is a 95% probability that the fixed (but unknown) true mean lies in this particular computed interval; rather, the method produces intervals that contain the true mean 95% of the time in repeated sampling.
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for a correct practical interpretation (interval for the true mean); 1 mark for avoiding/explicitly correcting the common misinterpretation about probability of the true mean for this specific interval.

performanceThresholds.fail: Incorrectly interprets the interval (e.g., treats it as a range for individual values or gives a fundamentally wrong probability statement).
performanceThresholds.pass: States it relates to the mean but interpretation is vague or includes a minor conceptual imprecision.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correctly interprets as an interval for the true mean with appropriate confidence wording.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Clear, technically accurate interpretation including the repeated-sampling meaning of 95% confidence and what it is not.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
To assess whether increasing oven temperature is associated with an output (e.g., defect rate/strength):
• Use a scatter plot to assess form and outliers.
• Quantify association with correlation (r) and/or simple linear regression.
• In regression, test H0: slope β1 = 0 versus H1: β1 ≠ 0 (or one-sided if justified) using the p-value and confidence interval for β1.
A statistically significant positive β1 supports an association that higher temperature corresponds to higher response (and vice versa for negative β1).
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for identifying an appropriate method (correlation and/or regression); 1 mark for identifying the correct inferential idea (testing slope/correlation, p-value/CI) and direction of association.

performanceThresholds.fail: Suggests an inappropriate method or makes a causal claim without evidence or statistical test.
performanceThresholds.pass: Mentions correlation/regression but with limited detail on how to decide association (e.g., no mention of slope/p-value/CI).
performanceThresholds.merit: Appropriate method with correct decision basis (slope/correlation and significance).
performanceThresholds.distinction: As merit, plus clear hypothesis framing (H0: β1=0), attention to diagnostics/outliers, and correct non-causal interpretation.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
A standard model for ‘time between failures’ (positive, continuous, often right-skewed) is the exponential distribution if the hazard rate is approximately constant, or a Weibull distribution if hazard varies with age.
Exponential: f(t)=λe^{−λt}, mean 1/λ, memoryless property.
Weibull: flexible hazard; shape parameter indicates increasing/decreasing hazard.
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for selecting an appropriate lifetime distribution (exponential/Weibull) consistent with time-between-failures data; 1 mark for a correct justification (e.g., constant vs changing hazard, positivity/right skew).

performanceThresholds.fail: Selects an inappropriate distribution with no valid justification.
performanceThresholds.pass: Selects a plausible distribution but provides little/no justification or confuses key properties.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correctly selects exponential or Weibull with a reasonable justification linked to hazard behaviour.
performanceThresholds.distinction: As merit, with clear statement of assumptions (constant hazard → exponential; variable hazard → Weibull) and correct key properties/parameters.

sectionA.modelAnswer:
If task duration T is Normally distributed with mean μ = 10.0 days and standard deviation σ (as given), then the probability of completing by a deadline d is:
P(T ≤ d) = Φ((d − 10.0)/σ).
If asked for a two-sided probability or a quantile, rearrange using z-scores: d = 10.0 + z_p σ (e.g., z_0.95 ≈ 1.645 for a one-sided 95th percentile).
sectionA.markAllocation: 2 marks: 1 mark for correct standardisation to a z-score (z=(d−μ)/σ) and identifying use of Φ; 1 mark for correct probability/quantile statement and correct handling of one- vs two-sided requirement as per the question.

performanceThresholds.fail: Does not standardise correctly and/or uses an inappropriate distribution approach.
performanceThresholds.pass: Correct general approach but with a minor z-score sign/arithmetic issue or unclear one-/two-sided handling.
performanceThresholds.merit: Correct z-score setup and correct probability/quantile method consistent with the question.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Fully correct with clear statement of Φ usage, correct tail selection, and correctly presented final probability/quantile in context.

sectionC.modelAnswer:
Expected approach (model validation and sensitivity audit for a production cost model):
1) Define scope and purpose
• State the model purpose (e.g., planning, quotation, budgeting), decision context, time horizon, and outputs (total cost, unit cost, cost drivers).
• Identify stakeholders and acceptance criteria (accuracy/precision, timeliness, governance).

2) Verification (build correctness)
• Spreadsheet/code checks: formula integrity, no hard-coded constants where parameters should be, consistent cell references, protected ranges.
• Dimensional/unit consistency: £/unit, hours, kg, batches; ensure conversions are explicit.
• Balance checks: totals reconcile; cost components sum to total; sign conventions correct.

3) Validation (representation of reality)
• Data audit: sources, dates, sampling frame, missing values, outliers, measurement error.
• Assumptions review: linearity, step costs, capacity limits, learning curves, scrap/rework rates; document rationale.
• Calibration: fit/estimate parameters using historical data; report fit statistics where appropriate.
• Back-testing: compare model predictions to observed costs on a hold-out period; quantify error (MAPE/RMSE) and bias.
• Extreme case and sanity tests: zero volume, maximum capacity, very high scrap; outputs should be plausible.

4) Sensitivity analysis
• One-way sensitivity on key parameters (e.g., labour rate, material price, yield, setup time, overhead allocation basis).
• Provide elasticity/impact: ΔCost or ΔProfit per 1% change; identify top drivers.
• Scenario analysis: best/base/worst; include correlated drivers where justified.
• Optional: tornado chart or ranked table of drivers.

5) Risk and controls (audit trail)
• Identify model risks: parameter drift, data refresh errors, version confusion, misuse outside valid range.
• Controls: version control, change log, peer review, locked formulas, input validation, automated checks.
• Recommendations: frequency of recalibration, monitoring KPIs, documentation pack (assumptions, data dictionary, limitations).

6) Communication
• Produce a concise audit summary: what was tested, results, limitations, and ‘go/no-go’ recommendation for use.
sectionC.markAllocation: 20 marks: (i) Scope, purpose, and outputs (3); (ii) Verification checks (4); (iii) Validation plan including data audit and back-testing (6); (iv) Sensitivity analysis design and interpretation of key drivers (5); (v) Governance/audit trail and recommendations (2).

performanceThresholds.fail: Provides a largely generic discussion with limited operational relevance; little evidence of structured verification/validation; minimal or incorrect sensitivity approach; lacks governance considerations.
performanceThresholds.pass: Outlines basic validation steps (some checks and some sensitivity) but with limited structure, weak linkage to model purpose/data quality, and limited actionable recommendations.
performanceThresholds.merit: Presents a structured and appropriate validation plan including verification, data/assumption checks, and a clear sensitivity analysis identifying key drivers; includes practical governance controls.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Comprehensive, methodical audit plan with clear acceptance criteria; robust back-testing and diagnostic measures; insightful sensitivity/driver ranking (and scenarios/correlation where relevant); strong governance, documentation, and clear decision-ready reporting.

sectionC.modelAnswer:
Expected approach (Monte Carlo risk simulation and risk register entry):
1) Define the model and uncertainties
• Identify the three stages/activities and their uncertain durations/costs.
• Specify probability distributions consistent with information given (e.g., triangular with min/mode/max; normal with truncation; lognormal for skew; beta-PERT).
• State assumptions: independence vs correlation; if correlation is plausible (e.g., shared resource/weather), model it explicitly.

2) Build the Monte Carlo simulation
• For each iteration: sample each stage from its distribution, compute total project duration/cost (sum or network logic if precedence exists).
• Use a sufficiently large number of iterations (e.g., 10,000+) and set/record random seed for reproducibility.

3) Summarise outputs
• Report mean, standard deviation, and key percentiles (P50/median, P80, P90) for total duration/cost.
• Compute probabilities of exceeding thresholds (e.g., P(T > deadline), P(Cost > budget)).
• Present distribution plots (histogram/CDF) or a clear tabulation.

4) Sensitivity / risk drivers
• Identify which input(s) drive total risk using rank correlation/regression on simulation outputs, or scenario-based comparisons.
• Highlight the highest-contributing stage(s) and explain why.

5) Risk register entry (minimum fields)
• Risk title and description; cause; event; consequence.
• Likelihood and impact (quantified where possible, aligned to simulation results).
• Risk rating (inherent and residual).
• Mitigations (preventive), contingency actions (reactive), triggers/early warning indicators.
• Owner, review date, and status.
• Link to quantitative evidence (e.g., ‘simulation indicates 22% probability of missing the deadline’).
sectionC.markAllocation: 20 marks: (i) Correct choice/justification of distributions and assumptions (6); (ii) Correct Monte Carlo structure and implementation logic (6); (iii) Output summary with probabilities/percentiles and clear interpretation (4); (iv) Driver/sensitivity identification (2); (v) Well-formed risk register entry linked to quantified evidence (2).

performanceThresholds.fail: Simulation approach is incorrect or not reproducible; distributions/assumptions unjustified; outputs not meaningfully summarised; risk register entry missing key fields or not linked to evidence.
performanceThresholds.pass: Basic simulation described with plausible distributions; some summary statistics provided; limited percentile/probability interpretation; risk register entry present but lacks quantification and/or clear mitigations.
performanceThresholds.merit: Appropriate distributions with clear assumptions; correct Monte Carlo logic; clear presentation of percentiles and exceedance probabilities; identifies key drivers; risk register entry is complete and evidence-based.
performanceThresholds.distinction: High-quality quantitative risk analysis: coherent modelling including correlation where appropriate; robust interpretation with decision-relevant metrics (P80/P90, deadline/budget risk); clear identification of drivers; exemplary risk register entry with quantified likelihood/impact, triggers, owners, and residual risk.

sectionC.modelAnswer:
Expected approach (pricing and capacity decision using regression evidence):
1) Data preparation and exploratory analysis
• Define response variable (e.g., demand volume, sales) and predictors (price, seasonality, promotions, competitor price, lead time, etc. as provided).
• Clean data: missing values, outliers, encoding of categorical variables; ensure consistent units.
• Plot relationships (scatter/line plots) and consider transformations (e.g., log-demand) if appropriate.

2) Regression modelling
• Fit an appropriate regression model (often demand on price and controls).
• Interpret the price coefficient (direction and magnitude) and assess statistical evidence (p-value/CI).
• Check diagnostics: residual plots, normality/heteroscedasticity, influential points, multicollinearity (VIF).
• Validate predictive performance (hold-out or cross-validation if feasible) and state limitations.

3) Convert demand estimates into financial outcomes
• Use the fitted model to predict demand at candidate prices.
• Apply capacity constraint: feasible quantity q = min(predicted demand, capacity).
• Compute contribution/profit: Profit = (Price − variable cost)×q − fixed costs (as provided), plus any capacity-related penalties or overtime costs.
• If multiple products/resources are involved, formulate the capacity allocation logic (e.g., contribution per constrained hour).

4) Recommendation
• Recommend a price (and output/acceptance policy) that maximises expected profit subject to capacity.
• Provide evidence: predicted demand, confidence intervals or scenario ranges, and sensitivity to key assumptions.
• Discuss operational implications (service levels, backlog, overtime, quality) and risks.

5) Communication
• Present a clear, decision-ready summary table (price → demand → constrained sales → profit) and a concise narrative conclusion with caveats.
sectionC.markAllocation: 20 marks: (i) Data handling and exploratory analysis (4); (ii) Regression specification, estimation, and interpretation of price effect (6); (iii) Model checking/validation and limitations (3); (iv) Integration with capacity and costing to compute profit for options (5); (v) Clear recommendation and justification (2).

performanceThresholds.fail: Regression is inappropriate or misinterpreted; capacity/cost integration is absent or incorrect; recommendation unsupported by quantitative evidence.
performanceThresholds.pass: Produces a basic regression and some interpretation; limited diagnostics; uses predictions loosely; capacity and profit logic partially correct but incomplete; recommendation is stated but weakly justified.
performanceThresholds.merit: Sound regression model with correct interpretation of the price effect and reasonable diagnostics; correctly translates predicted demand into constrained sales and profit; recommendation is evidence-based with stated assumptions.
performanceThresholds.distinction: Excellent end-to-end decision analysis: well-specified and validated regression (with robust diagnostics); clear handling of uncertainty (CIs/scenarios); rigorous profit maximisation under capacity; insightful discussion of operational trade-offs and risks; professional, decision-ready presentation.

step13.integrityAndSecurity:
Academic integrity and conduct

1. Academic integrity expectations
You are required to complete the summative examination honestly and independently. Your submission must represent your own work, produced during the assessment window, and must not be assisted by any unauthorised person, service, tool or material. You must comply with all instructions issued for the assessment, including any permitted resources list (e.g., calculator type, formula sheet, notes policy) and any restrictions on collaboration.

2. Plagiarism, collusion and other academic misconduct
Academic misconduct includes (but is not limited to):
• Plagiarism: presenting another person’s work, solutions, proofs, code, diagrams, or explanations (including from the internet, textbooks, repositories, or published solution banks) as your own, without appropriate acknowledgement where acknowledgement is permitted.
• Collusion: working with others, sharing questions or solutions, or dividing tasks, where the assessment is designated as individual.
• Contract cheating: paying for, requesting, or otherwise obtaining third‑party completion of any part of the assessment.
• Unauthorised use of generative AI, tutoring services, or “answer check” platforms where not explicitly permitted.
• Fabrication or falsification of working, results, or evidence.
• Unauthorised materials: use of prohibited notes, devices, communication tools, or additional accounts.
• Impersonation or facilitating impersonation.

Where referencing is permitted (e.g., in written explanations), you must cite sources clearly and consistently. For mathematical working, you must show sufficient steps to evidence understanding; copying a final answer or a proof without derivation may be treated as misconduct.

3. Identity verification and candidate authentication (online self-study delivery)
To protect the integrity of the award, identity verification may be required. Candidates must:
• Use only their own registered account and ensure their profile details match official identification.
• Be prepared to present a valid photo ID where requested, and/or complete platform-based authentication checks (e.g., webcam photo, live verification prompts, or secure login verification).
• Ensure the assessment is taken by the registered candidate only; no substitute or proxy test-taker is permitted.
• Maintain the security of login credentials and not share passwords or access tokens.

4. Secure assessment conditions and environment
Unless explicitly stated otherwise, you must complete the assessment in a private, quiet environment. You must not communicate with others about the live content of the examination during the assessment window. You must not capture, reproduce, or distribute any part of the exam (including screenshots, screen recordings, photographs, transcription, copying into external tools, or sharing via messaging platforms).

5. Randomisation, question rotation and technical security controls
As the assessment is delivered online, security controls may be applied, including:
• Randomised question ordering and/or selection from an item bank.
• Parameterised numeric values and scenario variants so that each candidate receives an equivalent but not identical version.
• Rotation of contexts (e.g., different datasets, graphs, or applied scenarios) mapped to the same learning outcomes.
• Limits on backtracking (where used), time-on-question logging, and integrity analytics to detect anomalous patterns.
• Automated similarity and authorship checks across candidate submissions.

All variants are designed to assess the same learning outcomes at a comparable level of difficulty. Attempting to bypass security features or reverse-engineer the item bank constitutes misconduct.

6. Suspected misconduct: investigation and outcomes
Suspected academic misconduct may be investigated in line with institutional regulations and applicable awarding-body policies. Evidence may include system logs, similarity reports, proctoring flags (where used), and expert review of working. Where misconduct is upheld, penalties may include (as appropriate): mark reduction, award of zero for the assessment, failure of the module/programme, requirement to resit under conditions, referral for disciplinary action, and/or withdrawal of certification. Candidates have the right to be informed of allegations and to respond, and may access appeals procedures in accordance with published regulations.

7. Reporting issues
If you experience a technical issue during the examination, you must follow the stated contingency process (e.g., capture error messages, note the time, and contact support immediately). Technical difficulties do not permit unauthorised collaboration or use of prohibited resources. Any suspected security breach or accidental exposure of exam content must be reported promptly.
step13.accessibilityProvisions:
Accessibility provisions and reasonable adjustments

1. Commitment to accessibility
The Maths Certification summative examination is designed to be accessible and inclusive. Reasonable adjustments may be made for candidates with disabilities, long‑term health conditions, specific learning difficulties, sensory impairments, neurodivergence, mental health conditions, or temporary injuries, in accordance with relevant UK legislation and institutional policy.

2. No reduction of academic standards
Adjustments are intended to remove barriers and enable equitable demonstration of the assessed learning outcomes. They do not lower academic standards, change the learning outcomes, or provide an unfair advantage. The level of mathematical demand and the marking standards remain the same for all candidates.

3. Time-related adjustments
Subject to approval and evidence where required, time-related provisions may include:
• Extra time (e.g., a percentage extension) to accommodate processing speed, reading, writing, or fatigue-related needs.
• Rest breaks (stop-the-clock where feasible) for candidates who require breaks due to medical or disability-related reasons.
• Flexible scheduling within the published assessment window for candidates with fluctuating conditions, caring responsibilities related to disability, or time-zone constraints, where this does not compromise security.

4. Alternative formats and presentation adjustments
Where appropriate, the examination and associated materials may be provided in alternative formats, such as:
• Accessible digital formats compatible with screen readers (structured headings, tagged PDFs/HTML where available).
• Enlarged text, high-contrast versions, colour-blind friendly palettes, and dyslexia-friendly formatting.
• Alternative representations of diagrams/graphs (e.g., descriptive text, tactile or raised diagrams by prior arrangement) while preserving mathematical content.
• Captions and transcripts for any audio/video content used in questions.

5. Assistive technology and permitted tools
Candidates may use approved assistive technologies that support access without compromising assessment integrity, for example:
• Screen readers, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, magnification software, and alternative input devices.
• Specialist software for accessibility (e.g., dyslexia support tools) where these do not provide unauthorised solution generation.
• Accessible calculators or approved calculator accommodations, where calculators are permitted by the assessment instructions.

Use of any tool that generates or completes mathematical solutions (including unauthorised AI systems, solver websites, or automated proof/solution generators) is not permitted unless explicitly authorised as part of the assessment design.

6. Alternative methods of response
Where the standard input method creates a barrier, alternative response arrangements may be approved, such as:
• Submission of handwritten working via scanned upload/photograph, with clear legibility requirements.
• Use of equation editors or LaTeX entry instead of handwriting.
• Oral clarification of answers where this is an accessibility requirement and where it can be recorded and assessed against the same criteria (where feasible and approved in advance).

7. Process for requesting adjustments
Candidates should request reasonable adjustments as early as possible and before attempting the examination, following the published process. Requests may require supporting evidence (e.g., professional assessment or medical documentation) and should specify the functional impact and the adjustment sought. Approved adjustments will be confirmed in writing and implemented through the online platform where possible.

8. Technical accessibility support
If you encounter accessibility-related technical issues (e.g., incompatibility with assistive technology), you should contact support promptly. Where issues cannot be resolved in time, the programme team will consider appropriate mitigations (e.g., rescheduling within the window or provision of an alternative format), provided exam security and fairness can be maintained.

9. Fitness to sit and mitigating circumstances
If unexpected circumstances arise that materially affect your performance (including acute illness or disability flare-up), you should follow the mitigating circumstances procedure. Evidence may be required. Mitigation does not guarantee a mark change but may result in an authorised deferral or a further attempt, in line with regulations.
